visual.caption: The principles of this chapter in three groups.

slides.narration: Welcome to Class eleven accounts. Every shop, workshop and school keeps its books by shared rules, called generally accepted accounting principles. In this part we meet the basic concepts, such as the business entity, the going concern and the dual aspect, and the later principles such as matching, prudence and consistency. We apply each one to imagined businesses so that the idea becomes easy to spot in a question.

slides.heading: GAAP: the common rulebook
slides.body_md: GAAP make the accounts of different firms uniform, so readers can compare and trust them.

rows: The concepts, rules and conventions used to record transactions and prepare statements
Uniform accounts that can be compared and relied on
Owners, lenders, investors, tax officers and employees

visual.alt: Table of GAAP: full form, what they cover, their purpose and the users who gain

slides.narration: Generally accepted accounting principles are the concepts, rules and conventions used to record transactions and prepare statements. Their purpose is uniformity. When two firms follow the same principles, an owner, a lender or a tax officer can compare their accounts and rely on them. In this chapter we group the principles into those about the firm, about recording and about reporting.

slides.heading: The firm: entity, money and continuity

rows: The business is a unit separate from its owner
A watch bought for the owner from the firm's bank is drawings
Only events stated in money are recorded
A kiln bought for ₹68,000 is recorded; a potter's fame is not
The firm is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future
An oven is written off over its life, not valued at a hurried-sale price

visual.alt: Table of the business entity, money measurement and going concern concepts with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Three concepts describe the firm. The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so a watch bought for the owner from the firm is drawings. Money measurement records only events stated in money, so a kiln is recorded but a potter's fame is not. The going concern concept assumes the firm will continue, so an oven is written off over its life.

slides.heading: Quick check: whose payment is it?
slides.body_md: A weaving centre pays for the owner's wristwatch from its bank account.
slides.narration: Read the situation carefully. Ask who benefits from the payment, the centre or its owner, and how the business entity concept treats a payment made for the owner personally.

slides.heading: Period and historical cost

rows: Profit and position are found at fixed intervals, usually twelve months
An asset is recorded at the price actually paid and later market rises are not recorded
A godown bought for ₹16,00,000 stays at that figure

visual.alt: Table of the accounting period and historical cost concepts with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: The accounting period concept says profit and position are found at fixed intervals, usually twelve months, so owners need not wait until the business closes. The historical cost concept records an asset at the price actually paid. Later rises in market value are not recorded, because the price paid can be proved from a bill, while a market value is an opinion that keeps changing.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cost against market value
slides.body_md: **Kalahandi Millet Mart**, an imagined firm, bought a godown. A broker says it would now sell for more.
bullets: The balance sheet shows **₹16,00,000**, the price paid.
The rise of ₹4,00,000 is not recorded until the godown is sold.
Cost can be verified; a market value is an opinion.

rows: Rise as a per cent of cost

visual.alt: Table for Kalahandi Millet Mart: godown recorded at cost 16,00,000 rupees, market value 20,00,000 rupees, unrecorded rise 4,00,000 rupees, which is 25 per cent of cost

slides.narration: Kalahandi Millet Mart bought a godown for rupees sixteen lakh. A broker says it would now sell for rupees twenty lakh. Under the historical cost concept the balance sheet still shows rupees sixteen lakh. The rise of rupees four lakh, which is a quarter of the cost, is not recorded because the godown has not been sold. The price paid is proved by the deed and the payment.

slides.heading: Dual aspect: the basis of the equation
slides.body_md: Every transaction has **two aspects** of equal value, so Assets = Liabilities + Capital after every transaction.

visual.alt: Flow: every transaction has two aspects of equal value, so assets equal liabilities plus capital
visual.caption: Two sides, always equal.

slides.narration: The dual aspect concept says that every transaction has two aspects of equal value. When a firm buys machinery for cash, one asset rises and another falls by the same amount. When it buys goods on credit, an asset and a liability rise together. So assets always equal liabilities plus capital, and this accounting equation is the basis of double entry.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the equation, step by step
slides.body_md: **Lunglei Bamboo Works**, an imagined firm, starts with cash as capital. After each step, assets equal liabilities plus capital.
bullets: Machinery for cash swaps one asset for another.
A credit purchase raises an asset and a liability together.
A sale at a gain raises cash and capital while stock falls.

rows: Owner starts the firm with cash ₹2,00,000
Took a bank loan in cash ₹30,000
Owner withdrew cash ₹8,000 for personal use

visual.alt: Accounting equation table for Lunglei Bamboo Works: after seven transactions cash is 1,73,000, machinery 60,000, stock 25,000, creditors 30,000, bank loan 30,000 and capital 1,98,000 rupees; assets of 2,58,000 equal liabilities plus capital

slides.narration: Lunglei Bamboo Works starts with rupees two lakh in cash as capital. Machinery for cash only swaps one asset for another. Goods on credit and a bank loan raise an asset and a liability together. Paying a creditor lowers cash and creditors. Drawings lower cash and capital. A sale at a gain raises capital. At the end, assets of rupees two lakh fifty eight thousand equal outside liabilities plus capital of rupees one lakh ninety eight thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: going concern
slides.body_md: A firm has resolved to close at the end of the month.
slides.narration: Think about what the going concern concept assumes. If a firm has already decided to close, is that assumption still true, and what should its machinery then be valued at?

slides.heading: Accrual: record when earned or incurred

rows: Goods sold on credit on 27 March, cash received on 14 April
Revenue is earned when the sale is made
March electricity, bill paid on 20 April
The expense is incurred when the power is used
Fees taken in March for April classes
The service has not yet been given

visual.alt: Table of the accrual concept: three events, the year in which each is recorded and the reason

slides.narration: The accrual concept says revenue is recorded when it is earned and an expense when it is incurred, whether or not cash has moved. A credit sale made in March belongs to March even if the cash comes in April. Electricity used in March is a March expense even if the bill is paid later. Fees taken in advance belong to the later period.

slides.heading: Revenue recognition and matching

rows: Revenue is recognised when it is earned, that is when the sale is made or the service is rendered
A wardrobe delivered on 29 January and paid for in March is January revenue
The expenses of a period are set against the revenue they helped to earn in that period
A premium for twelve months is charged only for the months used

visual.alt: Table of revenue recognition and matching with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Revenue recognition, also called realisation, says revenue belongs to the period in which it is earned, that is when the sale is made or the service is rendered. An order alone earns nothing. The matching concept then sets against that revenue the expenses that helped to earn it. A premium paid for twelve months is charged only for the months used, and the rest is carried forward.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: profit of a month by matching
slides.body_md: **Theni Banana Chips**, an imagined firm, March 2027. Revenue is that earned in the month; expenses are those of the month only.
bullets: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock = ₹1,40,000.
Insurance paid of ₹36,000 covers twelve months, so ₹3,000 is charged and ₹33,000 carried forward.

rows: Revenue earned: sales of the month
Less: insurance of March only (36,000 paid for 12 months)

visual.alt: Matching table for Theni Banana Chips, March 2027: sales 2,40,000, cost of goods sold 1,40,000, wages 28,000, insurance 3,000, power 9,000, profit 60,000 rupees

slides.narration: Theni Banana Chips earned sales of rupees two lakh forty thousand in March. Cost of goods sold is opening stock plus purchases less closing stock, which is rupees one lakh forty thousand. Wages of the month are rupees twenty eight thousand, including the part still due. The premium covers twelve months, so only rupees three thousand is charged. With power, the profit of the month is rupees sixty thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit by matching
slides.body_md: Find the profit by charging only the expenses that belong to the month.
slides.narration: Work in steps. First find the cost of goods sold. Then find the wages and rent that belong to the month alone, adjusting for amounts of other months. Finally subtract every expense of the month from the sales.

slides.heading: Disclosure, objectivity and materiality

rows: Every fact that could influence users is shown in the statements or in notes
An uncertain court claim is reported in a note
Entries rest on evidence that can be checked, free from personal bias
A purchase is entered on the supplier's invoice
Items that could influence decisions are shown with care; trivial items are simplified
A packet of paper clips is expensed at once

visual.alt: Table of full disclosure, verifiable objectivity and materiality with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Full disclosure asks that every fact that could influence users be shown, in the statements or in notes, such as an uncertain court claim. Verifiable objectivity asks that every entry rest on evidence that can be checked, such as an invoice. Materiality says that important items must be shown with care, while a trivial item such as a packet of paper clips may simply be expensed.

slides.heading: Consistency, timeliness and industry practice

rows: The same methods are followed from period to period; a change needs a reason and disclosure
Depreciation is charged by one method every year
Information is recorded and reported promptly, so it is useful when decisions are made
Transactions are entered as they occur, not months later
The peculiar features of a trade may justify a treatment that differs from the general one
A dealer in an exchange-traded metal values stock at the day's price, as the trade does

visual.alt: Table of consistency, timeliness and industry practice with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Consistency asks a firm to follow the same methods from period to period, so that results of different years can be compared. A method may change for a good reason, but the change must be disclosed. Timeliness asks that information be recorded and reported promptly, while it is useful. Industry practice recognises that some trades have peculiar features, so the accepted practice of that trade may be followed.

slides.heading: Prudence and substance over legal form

rows: Provide for all likely losses; do not anticipate any profit
Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value
A transaction is recorded by its economic reality, not only its legal appearance
A van used under hire purchase is the buyer's asset from the first day

visual.alt: Table of prudence and substance over legal form with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Prudence, also called conservatism, asks the accountant to provide for all likely losses but not to anticipate any profit. That is why closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Substance over legal form says a transaction is recorded by its economic reality. A van used under a hire purchase agreement is the user's asset from the first day, though the seller keeps legal title.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value
slides.body_md: **Ghatsila Appliances**, an imagined shop, values each line of closing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
bullets: Mixer grinders and water purifiers stay at cost: the expected gain is not recorded.
Induction plates and hair dryers are written down: a loss of ₹13,000 is provided for.

visual.alt: Table for Ghatsila Appliances: stock of 1,27,000 rupees at cost and 1,25,000 rupees at net realisable value is valued line by line at 1,14,000 rupees, a write-down of 13,000 rupees

slides.narration: Ghatsila Appliances compares cost with net realisable value for each line. Mixer grinders and water purifiers could fetch more than they cost, but the gain is not recorded, so they stay at cost. Induction plates and hair dryers would fetch less, so they are written down. Stock at cost is rupees one lakh twenty seven thousand and the value taken is rupees one lakh fourteen thousand, a write down of rupees thirteen thousand.

slides.heading: Which principle applies?

rows: The owner's personal bill is paid from the firm's bank
A premium is charged only for the months used
Stock is valued below cost after a price fall
The same depreciation method is used every year
A tiny item is expensed at once
A purchase is entered only on an invoice
A hire-purchase van is shown as an asset of the user

visual.alt: Table matching seven situations to the principles they illustrate

slides.narration: Here are seven situations and the principle behind each. A personal bill paid by the firm is business entity. A premium charged for the months used is matching. Stock valued below cost is prudence. The same depreciation method every year is consistency. A tiny item expensed at once is materiality. A purchase entered on an invoice is verifiable objectivity. A hire purchase van shown as an asset is substance over legal form.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **GAAP** make accounts uniform and comparable.
About the firm: entity, money measurement, going concern, period, historical cost.
About recording: dual aspect, accrual, revenue recognition, matching.
About reporting: disclosure, objectivity, materiality, consistency, prudence and the rest.

rows: Business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, historical cost
Dual aspect, accrual, revenue recognition, matching
Full disclosure, objectivity, materiality, consistency, prudence, timeliness, industry practice, substance over legal form

visual.alt: Summary table grouping the principles into those about the firm, about recording and about reporting

slides.narration: To sum up. Generally accepted accounting principles make accounts uniform and comparable. Some principles describe the firm: the entity, money, continuity, the period and cost. Others govern recording, through dual aspect, accrual, revenue recognition and matching. The rest guide reporting: full disclosure, objectivity, materiality, consistency, prudence, timeliness, industry practice and substance over legal form.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the principle, then say in one line why it applies.
Say clearly whether the treatment follows or violates it.
In stock and matching problems, show every line of the working.

rows: Name the principle and give the reason it applies
Marks go to the reasoning as well as to the name
Show each line of a stock or matching working
Step marks are given even if the last figure slips
Say whether a treatment follows or violates a principle
Questions often ask for exactly this

visual.alt: Exam tips table for the principles of accounting

slides.narration: In the examination, name the principle and say in one line why it applies. When a question asks you to identify a principle, say whether the treatment follows it or violates it. In stock questions, compare cost with net realisable value for every line. In matching questions, charge only the months that belong to the period, and show each line of your working.

decks.title: Accounting Concepts — Part 2: Cash and Accrual Bases, Standards and IFRS
goals: Distinguish the cash basis from the accrual basis and give the effect of advance, arrears, prepaid and outstanding items
Compute income, expenses and profit on both bases from one year's data and reconcile the two profits
Explain the meaning, need, advantages and limitations of accounting standards, and state what IFRS are, their objectives and the benefits of convergence

slides.heading: Two bases of accounting, and the standards behind them

visual.alt: Table of the cash basis and the accrual basis: when revenue and expenses are recorded

slides.narration: Welcome to Part two. The same year of a business can show two different profits, depending on whether we record by cash or by earning. We learn both bases, adjust one year of imagined data from cash to accrual, and reconcile the two profits. Then we study accounting standards, why they are needed, their advantages and limits, and the international financial reporting standards.

slides.heading: Cash basis and accrual basis

visual.alt: Table of the cash basis and the accrual basis: when revenue and expenses are recorded

slides.narration: On the cash basis, revenue is recorded when cash is received and an expense when cash is paid. On the accrual basis, revenue is recorded when it is earned and an expense when it is incurred, whether or not cash has moved. The accrual basis ties every item to the period it belongs to, which is why firms keep their books on it.

slides.heading: The same event on the two bases

rows: Fees for November received in October
Rent for March paid in April
Goods sold on credit in June, cash received in July

visual.alt: Table showing in which period three events are recorded under the cash basis and under the accrual basis

slides.narration: See how three events fall in different periods. Fees for November received in October are October revenue on the cash basis but November revenue on the accrual basis. Rent for March paid in April is an April expense on the cash basis but a March expense on the accrual basis. A credit sale in June paid in July is July revenue by cash and June revenue by accrual.

slides.heading: Quick check: when is it recorded?
slides.body_md: A firm on the cash basis sells goods on credit in March and is paid in April.
slides.narration: Recall what triggers a record on the cash basis. Is it the sale, or is it the receipt of cash? Then decide the month in which the revenue appears.

slides.heading: The four adjustments

headers: Effect on revenue or expense of the year
Balance sheet at the year end

visual.alt: Table of four adjustments: income received in advance, accrued income, prepaid expense and outstanding expense, with their effect on the year and on the balance sheet

slides.narration: To move from cash to accrual we make four adjustments. Income received in advance is deducted from revenue and is a liability. Accrued income, earned but not yet received, is added to revenue and is an asset. A prepaid expense is deducted from the expense and is an asset. An outstanding expense is added to the expense and is a liability. Amounts of the last year are also taken out.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one year on both bases
slides.body_md: **Pakyong Tuition Hub**, an imagined centre, year ended 31 March 2027. Each cash figure is adjusted to reach the accrual figure.

visual.alt: Table for Pakyong Tuition Hub, year ended 31 March 2027: fees 5,40,000 and 5,05,000, expenses 3,60,000 and 3,47,000, profit 1,80,000 on the cash basis and 1,58,000 rupees on the accrual basis

slides.narration: Pakyong Tuition Hub received fees of rupees five lakh forty thousand and paid expenses of rupees three lakh sixty thousand, so its cash profit is rupees one lakh eighty thousand. After removing advance fees and arrears of the last year and adding fees still due, revenue is rupees five lakh five thousand. After adjusting rent, salary and electricity, expenses are rupees three lakh forty seven thousand. The accrual profit is rupees one lakh fifty eight thousand.

slides.heading: How each figure was adjusted

rows: Less: advance received for the next year
Less: arrears of the last year received this year
Add: fees of this year still to be received
Less: rent paid in advance for the next year
Less: salary of the last year paid this year
Add: salary of this year still unpaid
Add: electricity of this year still unpaid

visual.alt: Adjustment table for Pakyong Tuition Hub: each cash figure is adjusted for advance, arrears, prepaid, last-year and unpaid amounts to reach the accrual figure

slides.narration: This table shows the adjustment behind every accrual figure. Fees start from the cash received, less the advance for the next year, less arrears of the last year, plus fees still due. Rent is reduced by the part paid for the next year. Salary is reduced by the part of the last year and increased by the unpaid part. Electricity is increased by the unpaid bill.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a smaller case
slides.body_md: **Dibang Agencies**, an imagined firm, earns commission and pays rent and wages.
bullets: Commission: remove what is received for the next year, add what is earned but not received.
Rent: remove the part paid for the next year. Wages: add the part unpaid.

visual.alt: Table for Dibang Agencies: commission 72,000 and 68,000, expenses 58,000 and 57,000, profit 14,000 on the cash basis and 11,000 rupees on the accrual basis

slides.narration: Dibang Agencies received commission of rupees seventy two thousand. After removing rupees nine thousand for the next year and adding rupees five thousand earned but not received, commission income is rupees sixty eight thousand. Rent and wages are adjusted in the same way, giving expenses of rupees fifty seven thousand. The cash profit is rupees fourteen thousand and the accrual profit is rupees eleven thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: accrual profit
slides.body_md: Adjust revenue and expenses for the year, then subtract.
slides.narration: Work in three steps. Adjust the fees received for the advance and for the fees still to come. Adjust the expenses paid for the prepaid and unpaid parts. Then subtract the expenses of the year from the revenue of the year.

slides.heading: Cash basis against accrual basis

rows: Revenue of the period less its expenses

visual.alt: Table comparing the cash basis and the accrual basis on revenue, expenses, outstanding and prepaid items, profit and the picture of the period

slides.narration: Here the two bases are compared. Revenue is recorded on receipt of cash, or when earned. Expenses are recorded on payment of cash, or when incurred. Outstanding and prepaid items are ignored on the cash basis but adjusted on the accrual basis. The profit is receipts less payments on one basis, and revenue of the period less its expenses on the other. The accrual basis gives the truer picture of a period.

sections.heading: 1. GAAP and the groups of principles
sections.body_md:
**GAAP** (generally accepted accounting principles) are the concepts, rules and conventions that accountants follow so that accounts are uniform. A reader can then compare firms and years and rely on the figures.

In this chapter the principles fall into three groups: those **about the firm** (entity, money measurement, going concern, period, historical cost), those **about recording** (dual aspect, accrual, revenue recognition, matching) and those **about reporting** (disclosure, objectivity, materiality, consistency, prudence, timeliness, industry practice, substance over legal form).

sections.heading: 2. GAAP I: the firm, its money, its life and its cost
sections.body_md:
**Business entity:** the business is separate from its owner; the owner's personal payments are **drawings** and reduce capital.

**Money measurement:** only events that can be stated in money are recorded.

**Going concern:** the firm is assumed to continue, so assets are written off over their lives and not valued at forced-sale prices; the assumption ends when closure is decided.

**Accounting period:** profit and position are found at fixed intervals, usually twelve months.

**Historical cost:** an asset is recorded at the price actually paid; later market rises are not recorded. **Advantage:** verifiable. **Limitation:** may understate current worth.

sections.heading: 3. Dual aspect and accrual
sections.body_md:
**Dual aspect:** every transaction has two aspects of equal value, so **Assets = Liabilities + Capital** holds after every transaction. A gain increases capital; drawings decrease it.

**Accrual:** revenue is recorded when earned and an expense when incurred, whether or not cash has moved. Typical effects: a credit sale is revenue of the sale year; a bill for power already used is an expense of the year of use; an advance is a liability until the service is given.

sections.heading: 4. GAAP II: revenue recognition and matching
sections.body_md:
**Revenue recognition (realisation):** revenue is recognised when the sale is made or the service rendered, giving a right to the price. An order or an advance is not yet revenue.

**Matching:** the expenses of a period are set against the revenue they helped to earn in the same period. **Format of a matching statement:** revenue; less cost of goods sold (opening stock + purchases − closing stock); less expenses of the period only (paid ± adjustments); equals profit.

sections.heading: 5. GAAP II: reporting principles
sections.body_md:
**Full disclosure:** every fact that could influence users is shown. **Verifiable objectivity:** entries rest on checkable evidence. **Materiality:** significant items are shown with care, trivial ones simplified. **Consistency:** the same methods period after period; a change needs a reason and disclosure. **Timeliness:** information is recorded and reported promptly. **Industry practice:** the peculiarities of a trade may justify its accepted treatment.

**Prudence:** provide for likely losses; do not anticipate profit; stock goes at the **lower of cost and net realisable value**. **Substance over legal form:** record the economic reality (for example a hire-purchase asset of the user).

sections.heading: 6. Cash basis and accrual basis
sections.body_md:
**Cash basis:** revenue on receipt of cash, expenses on payment. **Accrual basis:** revenue when earned, expenses when incurred.

**Adjustments to reach the accrual figure.** Revenue = cash received − advance for the next year − arrears of the last year + accrued (earned, not received). Expense = cash paid − prepaid − amount of the last year paid now + outstanding.

**Check:** accrual profit − cash profit = net adjustments to revenue less net adjustments to expenses. Both profits can be reconciled this way. The accrual basis gives the truer picture of a period.

sections.heading: 7. Accounting standards and IFRS
sections.body_md:
**Accounting standards** are written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies for the treatment and disclosure of items. **Need:** comparability, reliability, fewer alternative methods. **Advantages:** uniform practice, trust, easier audit, comparison by investors. **Limitations:** rigidity, cost, judgement still needed, revision as business changes. The other concepts concern the length of the reporting interval, proof for entries and the reporting of material facts.

questions.stem_md: Kalahandi Millet Mart, an imagined firm, bought a godown for ₹16,00,000 some years ago. A broker now says that the godown would sell for ₹20,00,000. Under the historical cost concept the balance sheet shows the godown at
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹16,00,000. The price actually paid, ₹16,00,000, is the recorded value. The broker's figure of ₹20,00,000 is an opinion that changes, ₹18,00,000 is a made-up average, and ₹4,00,000 is merely the unrecorded rise.

questions.stem_md: On 3 May 2026 an imagined trading firm collects ₹12,000 in cash from a customer who owed it that amount. By the dual aspect concept, the effect on the accounting equation is

options.text_md: one asset rises and another asset falls by ₹12,000, so total assets are unchanged
assets and liabilities both rise by ₹12,000
assets rise by ₹12,000 and capital rises by ₹12,000
a liability falls by ₹12,000 and an asset falls by ₹12,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** one asset rises and another asset falls by ₹12,000, so total assets are unchanged. Cash (an asset) increases and the debtor balance (another asset) decreases by the same amount. Liabilities and capital are not touched, which rules out the options that bring in a liability or capital.

questions.stem_md: Mokokchung Cane Furniture, an imagined firm, receives the electricity bill for March 2027 on 8 April 2027 and pays it on 20 April 2027. Under the accrual concept the expense belongs to

options.text_md: April 2027, the month in which the bill was received
April 2027, the month in which the bill was paid
neither month, until the next balance sheet date
March 2027, the month in which the electricity was used

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** March 2027, the month in which the electricity was used. On the accrual concept an expense is recorded when it is incurred, not when the bill arrives or cash goes out, so the month of use carries it. The date of the bill and the date of payment do not decide the period.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After every transaction of an imagined firm, the total of its assets equals the total of its liabilities and capital.

**Reason (R):** Every transaction has two aspects of equal value, so each change on one side of the equation is matched by an equal change on the other.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. The two equal aspects of a transaction are exactly why the equation stays in balance, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.stem_md: Ashoka Pens, an imagined firm, has resolved to close down at the end of the month. It should still value its machinery as if it will be used for many more years under the going concern concept.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The going concern concept holds only while continuity is assumed. Once closure is decided, the assumption fails and machinery is valued at what it will fetch on disposal.

questions.stem_md: Vanshika Traders, an imagined firm, bought land for ₹5,00,000 in 2019. Because the same land now sells for ₹9,00,000, the historical cost concept requires the land to be raised in the books to ₹9,00,000.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** An asset stays at the price actually paid. A rise in market value is not recorded until a transaction takes place.

questions.stem_md: The concept that treats a business as a unit separate from its owner is the ______ concept, and cash taken by the owner for personal use is called ______.
questions.solution_md: The business entity concept separates the business from the owner, and personal withdrawals are drawings.

questions.stem_md: At the year end an imagined firm, Pathar Cutlery, has cash ₹1,10,000, stock ₹90,000, debtors ₹70,000 and furniture ₹60,000. It owes creditors ₹45,000 and a bank loan of ₹55,000. Using the accounting equation, find the owner's capital (in ₹).
Nabarang Tools, an imagined firm, sells on credit goods that cost ₹34,000 for ₹46,500. Treating the sale through the accounting equation, by how much does the owner's capital increase (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Debtors rise by 46,500 and stock falls by 34,000. The two sides must stay equal, so capital rises by 46,500 − 34,000 = ₹12,500.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by GAAP? Why are the accounts of different firms prepared according to them?
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then the purpose of uniformity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**GAAP** (generally accepted accounting principles) are the rules, concepts and conventions that accountants follow when they record transactions and prepare financial statements.

They are followed so that accounts are uniform and the statements of different firms and years can be compared and relied on.

questions.stem_md: Ramesh Verma pays his son's school fee of ₹6,000 from the cash box of Verma Carpets, an imagined firm. How does the business entity concept treat the payment? State its effect on cash and on capital.
questions.solution_md: Drawings, with both effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
The firm and its owner are separate. The fee is a personal payment, so it is **drawings**, not an expense of the firm.

Cash falls by ₹6,000 and capital falls by ₹6,000.

marking_scheme.step: Treated as drawings, not as a business expense
Cash and capital each reduced by ₹6,000

questions.stem_md: Explain the going concern concept with one effect it has on the way a firm shows its machinery.
questions.solution_md: The assumption and one effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **going concern** concept assumes that the firm will carry on its activities for the foreseeable future and will not be closed or sharply reduced.

As a result machinery is shown at cost less depreciation and is written off over its useful life, not valued at the price a forced sale would bring.

marking_scheme.step: Effect on machinery: cost less depreciation over its life

questions.stem_md: Explain the dual aspect concept. Show how it affects the assets, liabilities and capital of an imagined firm when it (i) buys a typewriter on credit for ₹14,000, and (ii) repays ₹5,000 of a bank loan in cash.
questions.solution_md: The concept, then one equal pair of effects for each transaction.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **dual aspect** concept: every transaction has two aspects of equal value, so Assets = Liabilities + Capital after every transaction.

(i) Typewriter on credit: an asset (typewriter) rises by ₹14,000 and a liability (creditors) rises by ₹14,000.

(ii) Loan repaid in cash: an asset (cash) falls by ₹5,000 and a liability (bank loan) falls by ₹5,000.

marking_scheme.step: Credit purchase: asset and liability both up by ₹14,000
Loan repayment: asset and liability both down by ₹5,000

questions.stem_md: State the historical cost concept. Give one advantage and one limitation of recording assets at cost.
questions.solution_md: Statement, one advantage, one limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
Under the **historical cost** concept an asset is recorded at the price actually paid to acquire it, and later changes in its market value are not recorded.

**Advantage:** the figure can be verified from the bill and the payment, so it is objective and free from personal opinion.

**Limitation:** in times of rising prices the balance sheet shows values below current worth, so the position of the firm may look weaker than it is.

questions.stem_md: State the accrual concept. For an imagined firm with the year ending on 31 March 2027, say in which year each is recorded: (i) goods sold on credit on 27 March 2027, cash received on 14 April 2027; (ii) rent for March 2027 paid on 5 April 2027.
questions.solution_md: Statement, then year of recording for each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **accrual** concept: revenues are recorded when they are earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash is received or paid at that time.

(i) The sale is made on 27 March 2027, so the revenue belongs to the year ending 31 March 2027. The amount is a debtor at the year end.

(ii) The rent is for March 2027, so it is an expense of the year ending 31 March 2027, and the unpaid amount is outstanding rent.

marking_scheme.step: Sale recorded in the year ended 31 March 2027
Rent of March recorded in the same year as outstanding

questions.stem_md: Lunglei Bamboo Works, an imagined firm, began with cash of ₹2,00,000 brought in by the owner. It then (a) bought machinery for cash ₹60,000, (b) bought goods on credit ₹45,000, (c) took a bank loan in cash ₹30,000, (d) paid ₹15,000 to a creditor, (e) the owner withdrew ₹8,000 cash for personal use, and (f) goods costing ₹20,000 were sold for cash ₹26,000. Show the effect of each transaction on the accounting equation in tabular form and state the total of assets and the capital at the end.
questions.solution_md: Run the equation transaction by transaction, check the balance each time, then state the totals.

marking_scheme.step: Opening cash and capital; purchase of machinery and goods on credit
Loan and payment to the creditor
Sale: cash up, stock down, capital up by the gain
Closing total of assets and capital, equation agreeing

questions.stem_md: Lakhimpur Carpentry, an imagined workshop, received an order for a wardrobe on 10 January 2027, delivered it on 29 January 2027 on credit for ₹28,500, and was paid on 3 March 2027. By the revenue recognition concept the revenue of ₹28,500 belongs to

options.text_md: the month in which the order was received
January 2027, the month of delivery
March 2027, the month of payment
January and March, in equal parts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** January 2027, the month of delivery. Revenue is earned when the goods pass to the customer and the right to the price arises. A mere order earns nothing, and the date of cash does not matter.

questions.stem_md: On 1 October 2026 Pallavi Dairy, an imagined business, paid an insurance premium of ₹18,000 for twelve months. At the year end on 31 March 2027, the amount charged to the profit and loss account for the year, by the matching concept, is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹9,000. Only the six months used belong to the year: 18,000 ÷ 12 × 6 = ₹9,000. The whole premium would charge unused months, one month's cost covers a single month, and nil ignores the cover already used.

questions.stem_md: A customer has filed a suit against Jaunpur Textiles, an imagined firm, claiming ₹2,50,000 as damages, and the outcome is uncertain on the balance sheet date. To follow the convention of full disclosure, the firm should

options.text_md: say nothing until the court decides
report the claim in a note to its financial statements
record the ₹2,50,000 as a sale
reduce its capital by ₹2,50,000 and make no mention

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** report the claim in a note to its financial statements. A fact that could influence the decisions of a lender or investor is shown, in a note where it cannot be put in figures. Silence hides it, and a sale or a silent cut in capital misstates the position.

questions.stem_md: Hosdurg Pulses, an imagined firm, enters a purchase of goods in its books. Under the verifiable objectivity concept the entry should be supported by

options.text_md: the owner's own estimate of the price
the manager's opinion of what the goods are worth
documentary evidence such as the supplier's invoice and the payment voucher
a verbal promise from the supplier

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** documentary evidence such as the supplier's invoice and the payment voucher. Entries must rest on evidence that two independent persons can check. Estimates, opinions and verbal promises vary from person to person.

questions.stem_md: At the year end an imagined firm expects to gain ₹40,000 from a lawsuit it is likely to win and to lose ₹25,000 on a debtor who is likely to default. Following the prudence concept, the firm should

options.text_md: record both the gain and the loss
record the gain of ₹40,000 and ignore the loss
record neither until both are settled
provide for the loss of ₹25,000 and not record the gain of ₹40,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** provide for the loss of ₹25,000 and not record the gain of ₹40,000. Prudence provides for every likely loss but does not anticipate a gain until it is realised, so only the loss is recorded now. Recording the gain breaks the rule and ignoring the loss overstates profit.

questions.stem_md: Sehra Logistics, an imagined firm, uses a delivery van from the first day under a hire-purchase agreement, although the finance company remains the legal owner until the last instalment is paid. In keeping with substance over legal form, the firm should

options.text_md: keep the van out of its books until the final instalment
charge the whole price of the van as an expense of the year
record only the instalments as they fall due, with no asset
record the van as its own asset and the unpaid price as a liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** record the van as its own asset and the unpaid price as a liability. The firm controls the van and enjoys its use, so the economic reality is that it owns an asset and owes the balance. Legal title alone must not decide the record.

questions.stem_md: Parag Gold Traders, an imagined dealer in a metal traded on an exchange every day, values its closing stock at the day's exchange price because every firm in that trade does the same. This treatment follows

options.text_md: timeliness
the cost concept
industry practice
the money measurement concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** industry practice. Some trades have features of their own, so accepted practice in that trade shapes the treatment. Timeliness concerns speed of reporting, and cost would give the buying price instead.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An imagined firm provides for a likely loss on a doubtful debt in the current year but does not record a gain it merely expects.

**Reason (R):** The prudence concept requires all likely losses to be provided for while no profit is anticipated.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. The rule stated in the reason is exactly the practice described in the assertion.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firm that receives ₹50,000 in advance for goods to be delivered next month does not treat the ₹50,000 as revenue of the present month.

**Reason (R):** The revenue recognition concept says that revenue is recognised when cash is received.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is correct because the goods are not yet delivered. The reason is false: revenue is recognised when earned through a sale or service, which the advance alone does not make.

questions.stem_md: Under the consistency convention, Dharwad Plastics, an imagined firm, may change its method of charging depreciation if there is a good reason, provided the change and its effect are disclosed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Consistency forbids casual changes, not every change. A justified change is allowed when it is disclosed.

questions.stem_md: In keeping with prudence, closing stock is valued at the lower of ______ and ______, and so a possible ______ is provided for.
questions.solution_md: The lower of cost and net realisable value is taken, so a possible loss is provided for.

questions.stem_md: For June 2027 Dhar Spice Pack, an imagined firm, had sales of ₹1,80,000, opening stock ₹25,000, purchases ₹98,000 and closing stock ₹18,000. Wages paid in June were ₹15,000, including ₹3,000 of May, and ₹4,000 of June wages are unpaid. Rent of ₹20,000 was paid in June for four months starting June, and other expenses were ₹6,000. Applying the matching concept, find the profit of June 2027 (in ₹).

At the year end Kanker Appliances, an imagined shop, holds three lines of stock. Electric kettles cost ₹24,000 and could be sold net for ₹27,000; toasters cost ₹18,000 and could be sold net for ₹13,500; irons cost ₹15,000 and could be sold net for ₹16,500. Valuing each line at the lower of cost and net realisable value, find the value of closing stock (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Kettles 24,000 (cost is lower), toasters 13,500 (net realisable value is lower), irons 15,000 (cost is lower). Stock = 24,000 + 13,500 + 15,000 = ₹52,500.

questions.stem_md: What does the consistency convention require of a firm? Why does it help a reader who compares the profits of several years?
questions.solution_md: The requirement, then the benefit of comparability.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **consistency** convention requires a firm to follow the same accounting methods and policies from one period to the next, and to change one only for a good reason, with disclosure.

It helps because differences in profit between years then come from the working of the business and not from a change of method.

marking_scheme.step: Same methods period after period; change only for a reason, disclosed

questions.stem_md: Explain the materiality concept. Why may an imagined firm record the purchase of a packet of paper clips costing ₹40 as an expense at once, even though it lasts for several months?
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then why the small item is expensed.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **materiality** concept says that items large enough to influence the decisions of users must be shown separately and carefully, while trivial items may be treated in a simple way.

A packet of paper clips at ₹40 is too small to matter, so showing it as an asset and writing it off over months would cost more effort than it is worth.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: significant items shown, trivial ones simplified
Small item expensed at once because of its size

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between timeliness and industry practice as principles of accounting, with one line on each.
questions.solution_md: One line each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Timeliness:** accounting information should be recorded and reported promptly, so that users get it in time to use it for decisions.

**Industry practice:** the peculiar features of a trade may justify a treatment that differs from the general one, so the accepted practice of that industry is followed.

marking_scheme.step: Industry practice: treatment shaped by the trade's peculiarities

questions.stem_md: State the revenue recognition (realisation) concept. For an imagined firm, say whether revenue is recognised on each date: (i) a customer places an order for furniture; (ii) the furniture is delivered on credit; (iii) the customer pays the price later.
questions.solution_md: The concept, then the three dates.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **revenue recognition** concept: revenue is recognised when it is earned, that is when the sale is made or the service is rendered and the firm has a right to the price, not when cash is received.

(i) Order: no revenue; nothing has been sold.

(ii) Delivery on credit: revenue is recognised on this date.

(iii) Later payment: no new revenue; the debtor is simply settled.

marking_scheme.step: Delivery recognised; later payment not a fresh revenue

questions.stem_md: Explain the prudence (conservatism) concept with one example from valuing stock. How does it affect the profit reported for a year in which a line of stock has fallen in value?
questions.solution_md: Statement, example, effect on profit.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Prudence:** provide for all likely losses, and do not anticipate any profit.

**Example:** closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so a line that can now be sold only at less than its cost is written down.

**Effect on profit:** the write-down raises the cost of goods sold of the year, so the profit of that year is lower. A rise in the value of other stock is not recorded.

marking_scheme.step: Example: stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value
Effect: profit of the year reduced by the write-down

questions.stem_md: What is meant by substance over legal form? Show with the case of a machine bought on instalments, where the seller keeps legal title until the last instalment, how the concept affects the books of the buyer.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then asset and liability treatment.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Substance over legal form:** a transaction is recorded according to its economic reality and not only its legal appearance.

**Machine on instalments:** the buyer uses the machine and bears its risks, so it records the machine as an asset from the start.

The unpaid price is shown as a liability, which falls as each instalment is paid.

marking_scheme.step: Machine recorded as an asset of the buyer
Unpaid price as a liability, reduced by each instalment

questions.stem_md: Identify the accounting concept or convention followed or violated in each of the following imagined situations, with a reason: (i) Bhilai Footwear writes off a pencil sharpener costing ₹25 in the year of purchase; (ii) Sirsi Pickles records a sale on the day goods are delivered and not on the day the price is received; (iii) Alapuzha Ropes changes its method of depreciation every year to suit the profit it wants to show; (iv) Garhwa Stationers values a line of stock above its cost because its selling price has risen; (v) Nagda Motors enters a purchase on the owner's guess of the price, with no bill.
questions.solution_md: One concept and one reason for each of the five situations.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Situation | Concept | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| (i) Sharpener written off at once | Materiality (followed) | The item is too small to affect decisions, so it is expensed. |
| (ii) Sale recorded on delivery | Revenue recognition (followed) | Revenue is earned when the sale is made, not when cash is received. |
| (iii) Depreciation method changed every year | Consistency (violated) | Methods must be the same period to period unless a good, disclosed reason exists. |
| (iv) Stock above cost for a rise in price | Prudence (violated) | Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; no gain is anticipated. |
| (v) Purchase on a guess | Verifiable objectivity (violated) | Entries need documentary evidence such as a bill that can be checked. |

questions.stem_md: For the month of November 2026, Bhimtal Candles, an imagined workshop, had sales of ₹3,10,000, opening stock ₹55,000 and purchases ₹1,75,000. Its closing stock, with cost and net realisable value in brackets, is: candle boxes (₹40,000, ₹46,000), gift sets (₹30,000, ₹21,000), incense packs (₹25,000, ₹28,000) and lamps (₹20,000, ₹14,000). Salaries paid were ₹24,000 and ₹4,000 of November salaries are unpaid. Rent of ₹30,000 was paid on 1 November for three months, and other expenses were ₹12,000. (a) Value the closing stock on the prudence principle. [2] (b) Using the matching concept, find the profit of November 2026. [2] (c) By how much would the profit have been overstated if the stock were valued at cost? [1]
questions.solution_md: Value stock item by item, then match one month of each expense, then compare with stock at cost.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Closing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value:

| Item | Cost (₹) | Net realisable value (₹) | Valued at (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Candle boxes | 40,000 | 46,000 | 40,000 |
| Gift sets | 30,000 | 21,000 | 21,000 |
| Incense packs | 25,000 | 28,000 | 25,000 |
| Lamps | 20,000 | 14,000 | 14,000 |
| **Total** | **1,15,000** | **1,09,000** | **1,00,000** |

**(b)** Cost of goods sold = 55,000 + 1,75,000 − 1,00,000 = 1,30,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Sales | 3,10,000 |
| Less: cost of goods sold | 1,30,000 |
| Less: salaries (24,000 + 4,000) | 28,000 |
| Less: rent of November (30,000 ÷ 3) | 10,000 |
| Less: other expenses | 12,000 |
| **Profit of November** | **1,30,000** |

**(c)** At cost, closing stock would be 1,15,000, so profit would be 1,45,000, which is 1,45,000 − 1,30,000 = **₹15,000** more: the write-down provided for.

marking_scheme.step: Each line at the lower value; stock total
Cost of goods sold and the month's salaries, rent and other expenses

questions.stem_md: Tonk Kites, an imagined firm that keeps its books on the cash basis, sells goods on credit on 26 March 2027 and receives the price on 9 April 2027. The revenue is recorded in

options.text_md: March 2027, when the sale is made
April 2027, when the cash is received
both months, half in each
neither month, since the sale was on credit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** April 2027, when the cash is received. The cash basis records revenue only on receipt of cash, so the credit sale appears when the money comes in. The date of the sale does not matter on this basis.

questions.stem_md: On 10 March 2027 Barmer Tailors, an imagined shop with the year ending on 31 March 2027, received ₹30,000 in advance for stitching to be done in April 2027. On the accrual basis the ₹30,000 is

options.text_md: not revenue of the year ended 31 March 2027, and is carried forward as a liability
revenue of the year ended 31 March 2027
an expense of the year ended 31 March 2027
an asset of the year ended 31 March 2027

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** not revenue of the year ended 31 March 2027, and is carried forward as a liability. The work is not yet done, so nothing is earned and the firm owes the service, which is a liability. Counting it as revenue would apply the cash idea, and it is neither an expense nor an asset.

questions.stem_md: On 1 February 2027 Rewari Sound House, an imagined firm, paid ₹32,000 for an advertising contract that runs for eight months. The year ends on 31 March 2027. On the accrual basis, the expense of the year and the prepaid amount carried forward are respectively
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹8,000 and ₹24,000. Two of the eight months fall in the year, so the expense is 32,000 ÷ 8 × 2 = ₹8,000 and the rest, ₹24,000, is prepaid. The whole payment would be the cash view, the swapped figures reverse the two, and one month's cost counts a single month.

questions.stem_md: A trading firm records the following items for one year. Which one has the same effect on the profit of the year on the cash basis and on the accrual basis?

options.text_md: Rent paid in the year for the first two months of the next year
Fees of the year received in the next year
Salary of the last month of the year paid in the next year
Stationery bought for cash and fully used within the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Stationery bought for cash and fully used within the year. Only when payment and use fall in the same year do the two bases agree. The rent in advance, the fees received later and the salary paid later all cross the year end, so the bases differ for each.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On the accrual basis, salary of the last month of the year that is still unpaid is treated as a liability at the year end.

**Reason (R):** Salaries in most firms are paid at the end of each month.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but the usual date of payment does not explain the treatment. The salary is a liability because it was incurred in the year and not yet paid.

questions.stem_md: A firm that follows the cash basis shows no revenue in a year for goods it sold on credit in that year if it receives no cash for them before the year ends.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The cash basis records revenue only on receipt of cash, so unpaid credit sales do not appear.

questions.stem_md: Under the ______ basis of accounting, revenue is recorded when it is earned and an expense is recorded when it is ______.
questions.solution_md: The accrual basis matches revenue when earned and expenses when incurred.

questions.stem_md: During a year Sambhal Mats, an imagined firm that keeps cash-basis accounts, received ₹3,15,000, which includes ₹25,000 of advance for the next year. Its payments were ₹2,40,000, including ₹18,000 paid in advance for the next year. Find its profit on the cash basis (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: The cash basis ignores advances and prepayments. Profit = receipts − payments = 3,15,000 − 2,40,000 = ₹75,000.

questions.stem_md: Aizawl Sketching Classes, an imagined centre, received ₹1,20,000 in fees during a year, including ₹10,000 advance for the next year; fees of ₹14,000 earned in the year are still to be received. It paid expenses of ₹78,000, including ₹6,000 for the next year, and ₹9,000 of the year's expenses are unpaid. On the accrual basis, find the profit of the year (in ₹).

During a year Dindigul Bakers, an imagined firm, paid wages of ₹1,26,000, which include ₹14,000 that belongs to the last year. Wages of ₹9,000 for the last month of this year are still unpaid. Find the wages to be charged for the year on the accrual basis (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Wages = paid − last year's part + unpaid of this year = 1,26,000 − 14,000 + 9,000 = ₹1,21,000.

questions.stem_md: Churachand Agencies, an imagined firm, received commission of ₹64,000 in a year. Of this, ₹6,000 is for work of the next year and ₹4,000 is for work of the last year. Commission of ₹7,500 earned this year is still to be received. Find the commission income of the year on the accrual basis (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Income = received − next year's part − last year's part + earned but not received = 64,000 − 6,000 − 4,000 + 7,500 = ₹61,500.

questions.stem_md: Explain the cash basis of accounting. State one limitation of it for a firm that sells most goods on credit.
questions.solution_md: The meaning, then one limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
Under the **cash basis**, revenue is recorded when cash is received and an expense when cash is paid, whatever the period to which it relates.

**Limitation:** credit sales made in the year do not appear until the cash comes in, so the profit does not show what the firm actually earned in that year.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: recorded on receipt and payment of cash

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between income received in advance and accrued income, with one example of each from an imagined tuition centre.
questions.solution_md: Meaning with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Income received in advance:** cash received in this year for a service to be given in a later year, for example fees taken in March for April; on the accrual basis it is not income of this year and is a liability.

**Accrued income:** income earned in this year but not yet received in cash, for example fees of March still unpaid; it is income of this year and an asset (a receivable).

marking_scheme.step: Income received in advance: meaning and example

questions.stem_md: Ladakh Trekking Gear, an imagined firm with the year ending on 31 March 2027, paid rent of ₹60,000 on 1 January 2027 for twelve months. Find the rent chargeable for the year on the accrual basis and the prepaid rent, showing the working.
questions.solution_md: Apportion the payment by months.

answer.model_answer_md:
Months in the year ended 31 March 2027: January, February and March = 3 months.

Rent of the year = 60,000 ÷ 12 × 3 = **₹15,000**.

Prepaid rent = 60,000 − 15,000 = **₹45,000**, carried forward.

marking_scheme.step: Rent of the year ₹15,000 with working

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the cash basis and the accrual basis of accounting on any three points.
questions.solution_md: Three points of difference, one mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Point | Cash basis | Accrual basis |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | Recorded when cash is received | Recorded when earned |
| Expenses | Recorded when cash is paid | Recorded when incurred |
| Outstanding and prepaid items | Not recognised | Recognised and adjusted |
| Profit | Difference of receipts and payments | Revenue of the period less its expenses |

Any three points, one mark each.

questions.stem_md: Cuddalore Sports Club, an imagined club, paid rent of ₹48,000 in a year, which includes ₹8,000 for the next year. It paid salary of ₹30,000, which includes ₹4,000 of the last year, and ₹6,000 of this year's salary is outstanding. Find the rent and salary to be charged on the accrual basis and the total of the two.
questions.solution_md: Adjust each payment for prepaid, previous-year and outstanding amounts.

marking_scheme.step: Rent after deducting the prepaid part
Salary after deducting last year's part and adding the outstanding

questions.stem_md: Kasganj Dance Academy, an imagined academy, received ₹84,000 as fees in a year. This includes ₹9,000 received in advance for the next year and ₹5,000 that relates to the last year. Fees of ₹11,000 for this year remain to be received. Find the fee income of the year on the accrual basis, and say how it differs from the cash received and why.
questions.solution_md: Remove other years' amounts, add what is earned but not received, then compare with the cash figure.

answer.model_answer_md:
Fee income = 84,000 − 9,000 − 5,000 + 11,000 = **₹81,000**.

It is ₹3,000 less than the cash received (84,000 − 81,000), because the cash includes income of other years, which is removed, while only 11,000 earned but not received is added.

marking_scheme.step: Advance and last year's amount deducted
Accrued fees added to give the income
Difference from the cash received explained

questions.stem_md: Rudrapur Coaching Point, an imagined centre, closes its year on 31 March 2027. Salary of ₹15,000 and stationery of ₹3,000 of this year are unpaid. (a) Find the profit on the cash basis. [1] (b) Prepare a statement showing the income, expenses and profit on the accrual basis. [3] (c) State the difference between the two profits. [1]
questions.solution_md: Cash profit first, then adjust every revenue and expense item, then compare.

questions.stem_md: Sirmaur Photo Lab, an imagined studio, keeps cash-basis books and has found a cash profit of ₹1,40,600 for the year ended 31 March 2027 from receipts of ₹3,20,000 and payments of ₹1,79,400. The receipts include ₹18,000 of advance fees and ₹12,000 of arrears of the last year, while ₹22,000 of fees of the year are still due. The payments include wages ₹1,05,000 (with ₹7,000 of the last year; ₹9,000 of this year unpaid), rent ₹60,000 (with ₹10,000 paid in advance) and an insurance premium ₹14,400 (with ₹3,600 paid in advance). (a) Prepare a statement of profit on the accrual basis. [3] (b) Reconcile the cash profit with the accrual profit. [1] (c) Which profit gives a truer picture of the year's working? Give a reason. [1]
questions.solution_md: Adjust each line, reconcile through the net adjustments, then judge.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)**

| Particulars | Cash basis (₹) | Accrual basis (₹) |
|---|---|---|
| Studio fees | 3,20,000 | 3,12,000 |
| Wages | 1,05,000 | 1,07,000 |
| Rent | 60,000 | 50,000 |
| Insurance | 14,400 | 10,800 |
| **Total expenses** | **1,79,400** | **1,67,800** |
| **Profit** | **1,40,600** | **1,44,200** |

**(b) Reconciliation**

| Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Cash profit | 1,40,600 |
| Less: fees adjusted (3,20,000 − 3,12,000) | (8,000) |
| Add: expenses reduced (1,79,400 − 1,67,800) | 11,600 |
| **Accrual profit** | **1,44,200** |

**(c)** The accrual profit gives the truer picture. It counts only the fees earned and the expenses incurred in this year, whereas the cash profit mixes in amounts of other years.

marking_scheme.step: Wages, rent and insurance after adjustments

questions.stem_md: Several imagined shopkeepers in one town value their stock and charge depreciation in different ways, so their profits cannot be compared. The need that accounting standards meet here is

options.text_md: uniform treatment, so that statements become comparable
higher profits for every shopkeeper
avoidance of all taxes
removal of the need to keep books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** uniform treatment, so that statements become comparable. Standards lay down uniform rules and policies, which makes statements comparable and reliable. They do not raise profits, lower taxes or replace books.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a limitation, and not an advantage, of accounting standards for an imagined small firm?

options.text_md: Statements of the firm can be compared with those of other firms
The choice of alternative accounting methods is narrowed
A standard may be too rigid to suit every special situation of the firm
Users can place more trust in the reported figures

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A standard may be too rigid to suit every special situation of the firm. A fixed rule cannot fit every case, which is a drawback. The other statements describe benefits: comparability, fewer alternatives and greater reliability.

questions.stem_md: International Financial Reporting Standards, as a set of standards, are

options.text_md: rules of one country's tax department for income tax returns
a list of accounting books every firm must keep
accounting standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board for use in many countries
standards of quality for goods sold across borders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** accounting standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board for use in many countries. IFRS are a common set of accounting standards issued by an international body so that financial statements can be understood across countries. They are not tax rules, a list of books or product standards.

questions.stem_md: Tezpur Rubber Exports, an imagined company in India, wishes to raise funds from investors abroad. How does convergence of its accounting standards with IFRS help it most?

options.text_md: Foreign investors can read and compare its statements with those of firms in their own countries
It is freed from preparing any financial statements
It need not follow the law of its own country
Its profit is automatically raised

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Foreign investors can read and compare its statements with those of firms in their own countries. Common standards make statements understandable and comparable across borders, which gives investors confidence. Convergence does not remove the duty to prepare statements, override local law or raise profit.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Accounting standards narrow the choice of accounting methods open to a firm.

**Reason (R):** The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India is a professional body of accountants.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the second does not explain the first. Standards narrow the choice because they lay down uniform rules and policies, not because of who the issuing body is.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** International Financial Reporting Standards are issued by the tax department of each country for its own firms.

**Reason (R):** Convergence with these standards makes the statements of Indian companies harder to compare with those of foreign companies.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. The standards are issued by an international accounting body, not by national tax departments, and convergence makes statements easier to compare across countries.

questions.stem_md: Because Mandla Weaves, an imagined firm, follows accounting standards, its accountant need not exercise any judgement in preparing the statements.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Standards limit judgement and the choice of methods, but they cannot cover every situation, so the accountant must still use judgement.

questions.stem_md: Accounting standards narrow the choice of ______ accounting methods, so the statements of different firms become more ______.
questions.solution_md: Standards reduce alternative methods and make the statements comparable.

questions.stem_md: IFRS stands for International ______ Reporting Standards, issued by the International ______ Standards Board.
questions.solution_md: The full form is International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board.

questions.stem_md: What are accounting standards? Name the body that formulates them in India.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then the issuing body.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Accounting standards** are written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies for the treatment and disclosure of items in the financial statements.

In India they are formulated by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India.

marking_scheme.step: Institute of Chartered Accountants of India

questions.stem_md: State what IFRS are and give one reason why countries move towards them.
questions.solution_md: What they are, then one reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**IFRS** are International Financial Reporting Standards, a common set of accounting standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board for use in many countries.

One reason: statements prepared on common standards can be compared across countries, which helps investors.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning of IFRS with the issuing body

questions.stem_md: An imagined owner of a small shop says: "Accounting standards are not suited to me." Give three limitations of accounting standards that could support the owner's view.
questions.solution_md: Any three limitations, one mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rigidity:** a standard is a fixed rule and may not fit the special situation of a small firm.

2. **Cost and effort:** following the standards and their disclosures needs time, trained staff and money.

3. **Judgement still needed:** some choice between methods remains and the accountant must still judge, so the figures are not free from bias.

(Other valid points: standards may need to be revised as business changes; law prevails where it conflicts.)

questions.stem_md: Explain three benefits of converging a country's accounting standards with IFRS.
questions.solution_md: Any three benefits, one mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Comparability:** statements of firms in different countries can be compared by investors and lenders.

2. **Easier raising of funds:** a company can seek money abroad because foreign investors can understand its accounts.

3. **Less duplication:** a group with units in several countries can prepare one set of accounts and not several.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of accounting standards. Why are they needed? State two advantages and two limitations of accounting standards.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and need, then two advantages and two limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Meaning:** accounting standards are written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies for the treatment and disclosure of items in the financial statements.

**Need:** (i) to make the statements of different firms and years comparable; (ii) to make the statements reliable by limiting personal judgement; (iii) to reduce the alternative methods open to accountants.

**Advantages:** (i) uniform practice across firms; (ii) greater trust of lenders, investors and other users; (iii) easier work for auditors.

**Limitations:** (i) a standard may be too rigid for every special situation; (ii) following the standards costs time and effort; (iii) judgement is still needed.

marking_scheme.step: Need for standards: any two reasons

questions.stem_md: Dhubri Metals, an imagined Indian company with buyers and investors in several countries, is advised to follow IFRS. (a) State what IFRS are and name the body that issues them. [2] (b) Give two objectives of IFRS. [1] (c) Explain two benefits of convergence with IFRS for Dhubri Metals. [2]
questions.solution_md: Meaning and issuer, two objectives, then two benefits tied to the firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** IFRS are International Financial Reporting Standards, a common set of accounting standards for use in many countries. They are issued by the International Accounting Standards Board.

**(b)** Two objectives: (i) to bring a single set of understandable, high-quality standards for use across the world; (ii) to improve transparency and comparability of financial statements.

**(c)** (i) Foreign investors and lenders can read and compare Dhubri Metals' statements with those of firms in their own countries, so it can raise funds abroad more easily. (ii) Its Indian and foreign units can follow one set of standards, so there is less duplication of effort in preparing group accounts.

marking_scheme.step: First benefit applied to the firm
Second benefit applied to the firm
